goal: Teach the developer to capture the WinUI 3 `Microsoft.UI.Dispatching.DispatcherQueue` on the UI thread and use it to marshal updates.
must_include: Says `DispatcherQueue.GetForCurrentThread()` must be called on the UI thread; it can return null on a ThreadPool/background thread.
Uses `Microsoft.UI.Dispatching.DispatcherQueue`, not WPF `Dispatcher` and not `Windows.System.DispatcherQueue` for this WinUI 3 app.
Captures the queue in a page/window constructor, app startup, or UI-thread-created service and injects/passes it into the view model.
Uses `TryEnqueue` to run UI-bound work back on the queue and handles a false return or shutdown case.
must_not: Blocks the UI thread with `.Wait()` or `.Result` to make the dispatcher available.
Creates a new dispatcher queue on the background thread for XAML UI access.
Tells the developer to use `System.Windows.Threading.Dispatcher` in a WinUI 3 project.
acceptable_alternatives: Pass `DispatcherQueue.GetForCurrentThread()` from `MainPage` to the view model constructor.
Register an `IDispatcherQueueService` singleton on the UI thread and inject it into view models.
Move the UI state update back to the page code-behind while keeping non-UI work in the view model.
solved: The answer changes the pattern so the view model receives a UI-thread `Microsoft.UI.Dispatching.DispatcherQueue` and uses `TryEnqueue` for UI updates.
partial: The answer names `DispatcherQueue.GetForCurrentThread()` but does not explain why the current background-thread call returns null.
notes: This is about UI-thread dispatching, not general task scheduling or dependency injection architecture.
